bib.title: Neural Networks and Deep Learning (Chapter 18, Computer Age Statistical Inference)
bib.venue: Computer Age Statistical Inference, Cambridge University Press (book chapter, pp. 351-374)

question: How do neural networks and deep learning work (architecture, fitting by backpropagation and gradient descent, autoencoders, convolutional nets, regularisation), and how do they relate to statistical regression?
contributions: Explains single and multi-layer feed-forward nets as nonlinear generalisations of GLMs
Shows worked MNIST (0.93% error) and CIFAR-100 (35% error) networks
Shows dropout and input distortion are approximately ridge regression

results.claim: The MNIST network (3 hidden layers) reaches just under 0.93% test misclassification, beating a random forest and logistic regression.
results.setup: MNIST, 60,000 train / 10,000 test, 28x28 grayscale, 784 inputs; 3 hidden layers (1024,1024,2048), h2o.deepLearning, ReLU, dropout, accelerated gradient descent
results.quote: just under 0.93% errors), and outperforms random forests (2.8%) and a generalized linear model (7.2%)
results.note: Fig 18.3 caption prints 'state-of-the art error rate of 0:93%' (decimal point rendered as colon in text layer); 93 misclassified of 10,000. Authors warn in footnote 2 that best reported rates on MNIST may be optimistic.

results.claim: A random forest gets 2.8% test error on MNIST.
A logistic regression / GLM gets 7.2% test error on MNIST.
results.note: Fig 18.4 caption prints 0.072 for logistic regression

results.claim: The MNIST network has close to four million weights and so must be heavily regularised.
results.quote: This network has close to four million weights

results.claim: A convolutional network with 13 layers and about 50 million parameters gets 35% test error on CIFAR-100 (best reported seen: 25%).
results.setup: CIFAR-100: 100 classes, 500 train + 100 test per class, 32x32x3; Algorithm 18.2 configuration; Theano
results.quote: Our network achieved a test error rate of 35% on the 10,000 test images
results.note: Parameter count: 'around 50 million parameters' (p.368). Best reported 25% in text.

results.claim: Null (random-guess) error for K equal-sized classes is (K-1)/K: 50% for two classes, 99% for 100.
Dropout with rate phi randomly zeroes each node and inflates survivors by 1/(1-phi); for linear regression the expected score equations give a generalised ridge regression (18.24).
results.setup: Linear regression, squared error, mean-zero variables, I_ij iid with E=1; Wager et al. 2013
results.quote: This can be shown to be a form of ridge regularization
results.note: Equations 18.23/18.24 lose minus signs and symbols in the text layer: sign unconfirmed

results.claim: Adding iid N(0,sigma) noise to the predictors (input distortion) is approximately equivalent to ridge regression on the original data.
results.quote: is approximately equivalent to a ridge regression on the original data

results.claim: Dropout rate increases with layer density in the CIFAR net, from 0 at input to 0.5 at the final fully connected layer.
results.quote: from 0 in the input layer to 0:5 in the ﬁnal, fully connected layer

results.claim: Without the hidden nonlinearity a neural network reduces to a generalised linear model.
results.quote:
without the nonlinearity in the hidden layer, the neural network would re-
duce to a generalized linear model

results.claim: With a binomial deviance loss a network is a penalised logistic regression, highly parametrised and penalised.
results.quote: albeit a highly parametrized and penalized one

results.claim: Single-layer autoencoder with identity activation coincides with PCA (W = V').
results.quote:
If g
is the identity function, these solutions coincide

limits: Chapter is expository: single MNIST and CIFAR-100 runs, no seeds, no variance, no ablations.
MNIST error rate may be optimistic because the test set has been used heavily (footnote 2).
CIFAR-100 net is 35% error vs best reported 25%; authors concede 'some way to go'.
Many hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, batch size, momentum) not given; h2o has ~20 tuning parameters left at defaults.
Dated: 2016 view that autoencoder pretraining is crucial/then not; no transformers, batch norm, Adam, residual nets.
Equations in text layer lost minus signs and Greek symbols: sign unconfirmed
practices: Prefer abundant hidden units and control complexity with weight regularisation rather than unit count (Section 18.2).
Do not penalise bias terms; regularisation is typically light mix of l2 and l1 (18.2).
Use random small starting weights, never zero, to break symmetry (18.2).
Use SGD mini-batches for efficiency on large data (18.2).
Use dropout at deeper dense layers with rate rising by depth, and input distortion for images (18.5).
Early stopping was originally primary tuning; with adaptive regularisation test error flattens and does not rise (Fig 18.4).
Treat NNs as prediction machines judged on benchmarks, not estimation or explanation (18.6).
